title: Does a run/walk strategy decrease cardiac stress during a marathon in non-elite runners?
authors: Hottenrott K, Ludyga S, Schulze S, Gronwald T, Jäger FS
journal: Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport
population: Non-elite marathon runners (22 men, 20 women) completing a marathon either with a run/walk strategy or running only (randomized experimental trial, repeated-measure design)
findings: Finish times were similar: 4:14:25 +/- 0:19:51 with run/walk vs 4:07:40 +/- 0:27:15 running only (p = 0.377), a mean difference of about 6 min 45 s.
BNP, CK-MB and myoglobin increased after the marathon in both groups (p < 0.001) and returned to baseline 4 days later; elevated cTnI was seen in only two subjects.
BNP (r = -0.363, p = 0.041) and myoglobin (r = -0.456, p = 0.009) correlated inversely with velocity at the individual anaerobic threshold.
The run/walk strategy reported less muscle pain and fatigue (p = 0.006) after the event.
Authors concluded run/walk does not reduce load on the cardiovascular system but allows similar finish times with less muscle discomfort.
limitations: Small sample; one marathon; walk ratio not given in the abstract; outcomes are biomarkers and subjective ratings, not injury incidence; no ultra-distance evidence. Allocation details are not given in the abstract.
implications: Offer a run/walk option for marathon-distance goals: similar finish time (about +7 min mean, not significant) and less muscle discomfort, with no cardiac benefit.
Do not market run/walk as protective of the heart; present it as a comfort and muscle-damage option.
Walk-interval ratios and effects for 50 km-100 mile events are not established by this paper; no change to ultra pacing is justified from it.
